title: Homily II — The tomb speaks

edition.locus: Migne, PG 96 (Paris, 1860), Homily II on the Dormition, col. 745 (PDF leaf 414)

source_text: Σὺ, ὦ τάφων ἱερῶν ἱερώτατε, μετά γε τὸν ζωαρχικὸν τοῦ Δεσπότου τάφον, ὃς πηγὴ ὑπῆρξε τῆς ἀναστάσεως· ὡς γὰρ ἐμψύχῳ σοι διαλέξομαι· ποῦ χρυσὸς ὁ ἀκίβδηλος, ὃν ἀποστόλων χεῖρες ἐν σοὶ ἐθησαύρισαν; ποῦ πλοῦτος ὁ ἀδαπάνητος; ποῦ τὸ θεοδόχον κειμήλιον; ποῦ ἡ ἔμψυχος τράπεζα, ποῦ ὁ καινὸς τόμος, ἐν ᾧ ἀφράστως ὁ Θεὸς Λόγος χειρὸς ἄνευ ἐγγέγραπται; ποῦ ἡ τῆς χάριτος ἄβυσσος; ποῦ τῶν ἰαμάτων τὸ πέλαγος; ποῦ ἡ ζωοτόκος πηγή; ποῦ τὸ πολυπόθητον σῶμα τῆς Θεοτόκου καὶ πολυέραστον; Τί ζητεῖτε ἐν τάφῳ τὴν πρὸς τὰ οὐράνια μετεωρισθεῖσαν σκηνώματα; Τί με τῆς φθορᾶς εὐθύνας εἰσπράττεις; οὔ μοι δύναμις τοῖς θείοις ἀντιτείνειν κελεύσμασι. Τὰς σινδόνας καταλιπὸν τὸ σῶμα τὸ ἱερόν τε καὶ ἅγιον, καί μοι τοῦ ἁγιασμοῦ μεταδεδωκὸς, καὶ μύρου, καὶ εὐωδίας ποιῆσαν ἀνάπλεων, καὶ θεῖον ἀπεργασάμενον τέμενος, ἀνάρπαστον οἴχεται, δορυφορούντων ἀγγέλων, καὶ ἀρχαγγέλων, καὶ πασῶν τῶν οὐρανίων δυνάμεων. Νῦν ἐμὲ περιέπουσιν ἄγγελοι. Νῦν ἐν ἐμοὶ θεία χάρις αὐλίζεται. Ἐγὼ νοσοῦσιν ἰατρεῖον ἀλεξίπονον πέφηνα. Ἐγὼ πηγὴ ἰαμάτων ἀέναος. Ἐγὼ δαιμόνων ἀλεξιτήριον. Ἐγὼ πόλις φυγαδευτηρίου τοῖς προσφεύγουσι πέφυκα. Προσέλθετε πίστει, λαοὶ, καὶ ποταμηδὸν ἀρύσασθε τὰ χαρίσματα. Ἀδιάκριτον τὴν πίστιν κεκτημένοι προέλθετε. Οἱ διψῶντες ἐφ' ὕδωρ πορεύεσθε, Ἡσαΐας παρακελεύεται, καὶ ὅσοις οὐκ ἔστιν ἀργύριον, πορευθέντες ἀγοράσατε ἄνευ τιμῆς. Ἐγὼ πᾶσιν εὐαγγελικῶς ἀνακέκραγα· Ὁ διψῶν νοσημάτων ἴασιν, ψυχικῶν παθῶν ἀπολύτρωσιν, ἁμαρτημάτων ἐξάλειψιν, παντοίων ἐπιφορῶν ἀλλοτρίωσιν, οὐρανῶν βασιλείας ἀνάπαυσιν, πίστει προσερχέσθω πρός με, καὶ ἀρυσάσθω ῥεῖθρον τῆς χάριτος πολυδύναμον καὶ πολύχρηστον. Ὥσπερ γὰρ τοῦ ὕδατος ἡ ἐνέργεια ἁπλῆ καὶ μία τυγχάνουσα, ὡς δὲ γῆς καὶ ἀέρος, καὶ τοῦ παμφαοῦς ἡλίου, ἑκάστῳ τῶν μετόχων διαφόρως πρὸς τὸ κατάλληλον τῆς φύσεως μεταβάλλεται, καὶ γίνεται ἐν ἀμπέλῳ μὲν οἶνος, ἐν ἐλαίᾳ δὲ ἔλαιον· οὕτω καὶ ἡ χάρις, ἁπλῆ καὶ μία τυγχάνουσα, ποικίλως καὶ ἀναλόγως πρὸς τὴν ἑκάστου χρείαν εὐεργετεῖ τοὺς μετέχοντας. Οὐκ ἐξ οἰκείας τὴν χάριν κέκτημαι φύσεως. Τάφος ἅπας δυσωδίας ἀνάπλεως, κατηφείας πρόξενος, εὐφροσύνης ἀντίπαλος. Μύρον πολύτιμον δέδεγμαι, καὶ τῆς εὐωδίας μετείληφα, καὶ τὸ μύρον οὕτως εὐῶδες καὶ δραστικώτατον, ὡς μικρᾷ παραθέσει ἀναφαίρετον δωρήσασθαι τὴν μετάληψιν· ἀμεταμέλητα γὰρ ὄντως τὰ θεῖα χαρίσματα· πηγὴν εὐφροσύνης ἐξένισα, καὶ ταύτης ἀένναον ἐπλούτησα τὴν ἀνάβλυσιν.
pass_a_gloss: You, O most holy (ἱερώτατε) of holy tombs (τάφοι), after at least the life-originating (ζωαρχικός) tomb of the Master (Δεσπότης), which was spring (πηγή) of the resurrection (ἀνάστασις); for as to one ensouled (ἔμψυχος) I will converse (διαλέξομαι) with you: where [is] the unalloyed (ἀκίβδηλος) gold which hands of apostles treasured in you? where the unspent (ἀδαπάνητος) wealth? where the God-receiving (θεοδόχον) heirloom/treasure (κειμήλιον)? where the ensouled table, where the new volume in which inexpressibly (ἀφράστως) God the Word has been inscribed without hand? where the abyss of grace? where the sea of healings (ἰάματα)? where the life-bearing (ζωοτόκος) spring? where the much-longed-for and much-loved body of the Theotokos? Why do you seek (ζητεῖτε) in a tomb her raised aloft to the heavenly tents/dwellings (σκηνώματα)? Why do you exact from me accounts (εὐθύνας) of corruption (φθορά)? There is not to me power to strain against the divine commands (κελεύσματα). Having left behind the linen cloths (σινδόνες), the sacred and holy body, having given me a share of the sanctification (ἁγιασμός), and having made [me] full (ἀνάπλεων) of myrrh/ointment (μύρον) and fragrance (εὐωδία), and having produced a divine sanctuary (τέμενος), is gone (οἴχεται) snatched up (ἀνάρπαστον), angels and archangels and all the heavenly powers escorting [it] as guards. Now angels attend me. Now in me divine grace lodges (αὐλίζεται). I have appeared (πέφηνα) to the sick a pain-averting (ἀλεξίπονον) surgery/place of healing (ἰατρεῖον). I [am] an ever-flowing (ἀέναος) spring of healings. I [am] a defence of/against demons. I am (πέφυκα) a city of refuge to those fleeing to [me]. Come forward (προσέλθετε) in faith, peoples, and draw (ἀρύσασθε) like a river (ποταμηδόν) the gifts (χαρίσματα). Having undoubting (ἀδιάκριτον) faith come forth. 'The thirsting, go to water,' Isaiah exhorts, 'and those to whom there is no silver, going buy without price (ἄνευ τιμῆς).' I to all have cried out in gospel fashion: 'The one thirsting for healing (ἴασις) of diseases, ransom/release from soul-passions, wiping out (ἐξάλειψις) of sins, removal of all sorts of assaults/afflictions (ἐπιφοραί), rest (ἀνάπαυσις) of the kingdom of heavens, let him come to me in faith and draw a stream (ῥεῖθρον) of grace very powerful and very useful.' For as the operation (ἐνέργεια) of water, being simple (ἁπλῆ) and one, and as [that] of earth and air and the all-shining (παμφαής) sun, is changed differently to each of the partakers (μέτοχοι) toward what suits its nature, and becomes in a vine wine, in an olive oil; so also grace, being simple and one, variously (ποικίλως) and proportionally (ἀναλόγως) to the need (χρεία) of each benefits (εὐεργετεῖ) those partaking. Not from my own (οἰκεία) nature have I acquired the grace. Every tomb [is] full of stench (δυσωδία), procurer (πρόξενος) of gloom (κατήφεια), adversary (ἀντίπαλος) of gladness (εὐφροσύνη). Very precious ointment I have received, and of the fragrance I have partaken, and the ointment so fragrant and most effective, as by small placing beside (παράθεσις) to bestow an that cannot be taken away partaking (μετάληψις); for truly unrepented (ἀμεταμέλητα) [are] the divine gifts; a spring of gladness I hosted (ἐξένισα), and its ever-flowing (ἀέναον) upwelling (ἀνάβλυσις) I have been enriched with (ἐπλούτησα).
pass_b_english: You, most holy of holy tombs (after, that is, the Master's tomb, the beginning of life, which was the spring of the resurrection), I will speak to you as to a living thing. Where is the unalloyed gold that the apostles' hands laid up as treasure in you? Where is the inexhaustible wealth? Where is the treasure that received God? Where is the living table? Where is the new scroll in which God the Word was written, beyond words, without a hand? Where is the abyss of grace? Where is the sea of healings? Where is the spring that gave birth to life? Where is the body of the Mother of God, so longed for and so loved?

Why do you seek in a tomb her who has been lifted up to the heavenly dwellings (Luke 24:5)? Why do you demand from me an account of corruption? I have no power to resist the commands of God. The sacred and holy body has left the linen cloths behind; it gave me a share in its holiness, filled me with ointment and fragrance, and made me a divine sanctuary, and it has gone, caught up, with angels and archangels and all the heavenly powers as its escort. Now angels attend me. Now divine grace dwells in me. For the sick I have proved to be a place of healing that wards off pain. I am an ever-flowing spring of healings. I am a defence against demons. I am a city of refuge (Numbers 35:6) for those who flee to me.

Come forward in faith, you peoples, and draw gifts in streams like a river. Come forward, holding a faith that does not doubt. 'You who thirst, go to the water,' Isaiah urges, 'and you who have no money, go and buy without price' (Isaiah 55:1). I cry out to all, in the words of the Gospel: 'Whoever thirsts for the healing of diseases, for release from the passions of the soul, for the blotting out of sins, for deliverance from every kind of affliction, for the rest of the kingdom of heaven, let him come to me in faith (John 7:37), and draw a stream of grace that has great power and serves many needs.' For the working of water is simple and one, and so is that of earth and air and the all-shining sun; yet it is changed differently in each of the things that share in it, to suit each one's nature, and in the vine it becomes wine, in the olive oil. So too grace, simple and one, does good to those who share in it in many ways, in proportion to each one's need.

I do not have this grace from my own nature. Every tomb is full of foul smell, a bringer of gloom, an enemy of gladness. But I received a very precious ointment and shared in its fragrance; and the ointment was so fragrant and so powerful that by being laid beside me for a little while it gave me a share in it that cannot be taken away; for truly the gifts of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:29). I welcomed as my guest a spring of gladness, and I have been enriched with its ever-flowing outpouring.

choices.note: Speaker: the preacher addresses the tomb to the end of the first paragraph; the tomb answers from 'Why do you seek' to the end of the section.
The source note puts the start of the tomb's speech at Τί με τῆς φθορᾶς;

I begin it one sentence earlier, at Τί ζητεῖτε, because that plural question answers the preacher's 'where is ...' and echoes the angel's words at the empty tomb (Luke 24:5); the paragraph break marks the change of speaker without adding words.

Printed margin: Isaiah 55:1 (quoted loosely and shortened from the LXX: ὅσοις οὐκ ἔστιν for ὅσοι μὴ ἔχετε, πορευθέντες for βαδίσαντες, and only ἄνευ τιμῆς from the LXX's longer close; rendered as printed);
'Rom. ii, 29' is printed so, but ἀμεταμέλητα ...
τὰ χαρίσματα is Romans 11:29, cited so.
Unprinted allusions cited because the wording is clear: Luke 24:5 (Τί ζητεῖτε, at a tomb);
John 7:37 (εὐαγγελικῶς ...
ὁ διψῶν ...
ἐρχέσθω πρός με, here προσερχέσθω);
Numbers 35:6 (the LXX phrase πόλις φυγαδευτηρίου).
Left uncited: 'the new scroll' (καινὸς τόμος) probably echoes Isaiah 8:1 LXX ('take a new great scroll and write in it'), a common Marian figure, but the wording is too short to be sure;
'the living table' (the table of the bread of the Presence, Exodus 25:23-30) is a figure, not a quotation;
'μύρον πολύτιμον' matches Matthew 26:7 / John 12:3 in wording only;
'ἀδιάκριτον τὴν πίστιν' may echo James 1:6.
The water simile (one working, wine in the vine, oil in the olive) resembles Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechetical Lectures 16.12, on the Holy Spirit; noted, not marked in the text.
'τῆς φθορᾶς εὐθύνας εἰσπράττεις' rendered 'demand from me an account of corruption', that is, ask the tomb to produce the decayed body a tomb normally holds;
Migne fn57 prints 'R.
φθορᾶς', the same word as the text (checked at 600 dpi, PDF leaf 414; the source row note's 'R.
φορᾶς' is a misreading of the footnote), so the note is self-contradictory as printed;
Migne's Latin 'Quid custodiae rationem a me exposcitis?' suggests the editor's text read φρουρᾶς ('of the custody'), with R. reading φθορᾶς.
The printed φθορᾶς, which the footnote also attests for R., is followed. fn56 Δεσπότου (R.
Κυρίου): no change to the English beyond 'Master' vs 'Lord'; printed Δεσπότου followed.
'ἰατρεῖον ἀλεξίπονον' rendered 'a place of healing that wards off pain' (the adjective qualifies the noun);
πέφηνα 'I have proved to be'.
'ποταμηδόν' rendered 'in streams like a river'.
